title: Pricing by hours per project for Plastering
audience: Plastering contractors and supervisors who quote for room replasters, patch repairs and ceiling work, and need a price that covers cost and earns a margin.
learningOutcomes: Calculate a cost per productive hour from the business's own figures
Estimate plastering hours, including preparation, mixing, coats, drying, set-up, travel and checking
Build a quote from hours, a rate and a margin, and state its basis and exclusions

instruction.heading: Why hours are the starting unit
instruction.body: Plastering is labour-heavy, and most of its time is visible: stripping and preparing the surface, mixing, applying and levelling each coat, waiting for the plaster to set and dry, and cleaning up. Once those hours are known, the cost, the margin and the effect of a scope change can be seen. A flat price with no hours behind it hides risk, and it is hard to defend when a client asks why a patch repair or a room replaster costs what it does. A vendor listing gives per-task ranges, such as $80 to $200 for a small hole repair and $300 to $800 for a large section of wall or ceiling (TradeRefer plastering page, undated, vendor listing, indicative only). Use them only as a sense-check against your own hours.

instruction.heading: Build the cost per productive hour
instruction.body: Take the total cost of running the business over a period and divide it by the productive hours in that period. Total cost includes wages with on-costs such as leave and superannuation, where your staff arrangements require them, vehicle running costs, plaster, sand, mesh, bucket and scaffold hire, equipment, insurance, administration and premises. Productive hours are the hours a plasterer spends on chargeable work, not the paid hours on a roster. Business.gov.au lists on-costs such as leave and superannuation as part of the hourly cost (Choose a pricing strategy, page metadata dated 1 October 2026). If a plasterer is paid for 40 hours and 30 are chargeable, the cost per productive hour is higher than the hourly wage. Use the business's own figures, not a vendor's hourly range.

instruction.heading: Estimate the hours
instruction.body: Break each job into tasks: each wall, ceiling, patch, reveal or cornice, and any preparation such as removing old finishes or treating a damp area. Estimate each task at a standard speed for your own team, then add mixing, drying and setting time between coats, set-up, pack-down, travel between sites and a checking allowance. Use ranges where the job is uncertain. Add a set allowance for delays outside your control, such as late access, weather that slows drying, or staff absence. One guide suggests adding 10 to 20 percent to job estimates for unexpected work (Xero Australia, How to price services, 3 September 2026). That is a general service-business range, not a plastering figure, so check it against your own records. After each job, record the actual hours and the reason for any gap.

instruction.heading: Turn hours into a price
instruction.body: Multiply the crew hours by the cost per productive hour to get the cost of the job. Add a margin that reflects your target and the risk in the job, such as a poor substrate, damp behind the wall, difficult access or a tight deadline. One author presents a gross margin of at least 20 percent as a floor, and says the right figure varies by business and market (Carters Trade Leader, 1 October 2025). That is one author's view. Apply your materials policy and your minimum charge. If a client wants a lower price, show which walls, ceilings or coats they are asking you to remove, which keeps the discussion on the work.

instruction.heading: Keep the quote honest
instruction.body: A plastering quote should state the scope (surfaces, plaster type, number of coats, finish standard), the hours or price basis, the exclusions, what the client must provide, and how long the quote is valid. Typical exclusions include electrical work, moisture or waterproofing repairs, painting, and any structural repair. Do not show the internal cost per hour unless your policy says to. Record every change to the scope and re-quote when it changes. NSW guidance says variations must be in writing and signed by both parties, and that almost all variations affect the price (NSW Consumer Building Guide, published 1 November 2025, web page modified 19 February 2026).

instruction.heading: Review your estimates
instruction.body: Compare estimated and actual hours for at least the first ten jobs of each type, such as a patch repair, a room replaster and a ceiling. If the gap is consistently above an agreed threshold, change the standard time, the margin or the scope rules. A pricing method is not finished when it is written. It is finished when actual hours match quoted hours closely enough for the work to make money.

procedure: Gather the year's total business costs and the productive hours achieved in the same period.
Divide total costs by productive hours to get the cost per productive hour.
Break the job into tasks and estimate each task time as a range.
Add preparation, mixing, drying time, set-up, pack-down, travel and checking as named lines.
Multiply total crew hours by the cost per productive hour, then apply the margin for risk and target.
Apply the materials policy and the minimum charge.
Write the quote with scope, hours basis, exclusions, client inputs and validity.
Record actual hours after each job and compare them with the estimate.

workedExamples.situation: Hypothetical figures, invented for this lesson and not market rates. A single-room replaster needs an estimated 10 crew-hours, including preparation, two coats and a checking visit. The plasterer's cost per productive hour is $65 (hypothetical). The target margin on price is 25 per cent (hypothetical).
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the cost of the job, what is the price at a 25 per cent margin on price, and what changes if the job needs 2 more crew-hours for a damp patch the client has agreed in writing to have treated as a variation?
workedExamples.reasoning: The cost is 10 crew-hours at $65, which is $650. A 25 per cent margin on price means the price is the cost divided by 0.75, which gives $866.67. The variation adds 2 crew-hours, or $130, so the cost becomes $780 and the price becomes $1,040. The plasterer adds the variation only after the client has approved it in writing, and records the reason in the job log.

equipmentAndPpe: Quote worksheet or spreadsheet with room-by-room hours
Time log for each job, with estimated and actual columns
Measuring tape or laser measure for wall and ceiling areas
Level, straightedge and moisture meter where the site provides one

commonErrors.error: Pricing from the hourly wage alone
commonErrors.prevention: Include on-costs, vehicle, materials, equipment, insurance and administration in the cost per productive hour.

commonErrors.error: Counting paid hours as productive hours
commonErrors.prevention: Use chargeable hours only when calculating the cost per productive hour.

commonErrors.error: Leaving out mixing, drying and set-up time
commonErrors.prevention: Name mixing, drying, set-up and cleanup as separate lines on every quote.
List electrical, moisture and painting exclusions, and state the access assumptions.

commonErrors.error: Never comparing estimates with actual hours
commonErrors.prevention: Record actual hours after each job and review the variance monthly.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This is pricing guidance only. The Australian Consumer Law applies to pricing statements, and the ACCC says misleading statements about prices are prohibited (ACCC, Setting prices: what's allowed, last modified 15 July 2026). State and territory fair trading rules also apply, and they differ between states.

Plastering work can need a licence or registration, and the job value can decide it. In NSW, wet plastering needs a contractor licence for trade work valued over $5,000 in labour and materials including GST, and dry plastering is a separate listed category. In Victoria, plastering is a limited class of domestic building work, with separate classes for sheet plastering and for solid plastering and rendering. The Victorian sources read word the $10,000 threshold three ways ('more than $10,000', '$10,000 or more' and 'over $10,000'), and the single-trade limit for plastering-only or tiling-only work is not settled, so treat the threshold as unresolved and check it against the Victorian Act and with the Victorian Building Authority before use. In Queensland, solid plastering is a licensed class. Check the rule for each state where you work. This lesson does not grant any licence.

Pay rates, allowances and on-costs for employees may be set by an award or enterprise agreement. Check which one applies to each worker before using any cost figure. This lesson does not state those rates.

qualityStandard: Each quote shows scope, hours or price basis, exclusions, client inputs and validity.
The cost per productive hour is calculated from the business's own records and dated.
Actual hours are recorded for at least the first ten jobs of each type and compared with the estimate.
No quote is issued without a margin decision, a minimum-charge check and a licence check for the job value and trade mix.
documentationEvidence: Cost per productive hour worksheet, dated, with the source of each figure
Plastering quote showing scope, hours basis, exclusions and validity
Job time log with estimated and actual hours
summary: Hours make plastering work visible, so start every quote from hours.
Cost per productive hour uses chargeable time, not paid time.
Mixing, drying, travel and checking time are named lines, not hidden extras.
Compare estimates with actual hours, and change the method when they diverge.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which costs belong in the cost per productive hour?
options: Only the hourly wage of the lowest-paid plasterer, and nothing else from the accounts
The price the client pays, plus the deposit, the late fee and any bonus
The average hourly rate of competitors and the vendor listing ranges for the area
Wages with on-costs, vehicle, materials, equipment, insurance and administration, divided by chargeable hours

knowledgeChecks.question: A room replaster is estimated at 5 crew-hours and takes 8. What is the right response?
options: Leave the estimate, since the client has already paid and the crew has finished
Record the actual hours, find the cause, and adjust the estimate and future quotes
Reduce paid hours for the crew on the next job and skip the morning break
Raise the price for this client's next job only and no one else is charged more

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does a plastering quote need an exclusions list?
options: To hide the margin from the client and keep the rates secret from the crew
To make the quote longer and fill the page with more text
To show what the price covers, so scope changes can be priced and disputes are reduced
To lower the client's expectations and make the job seem smaller than it is
